The above activities will be tailored to meet the objectives of the urban renewal plan. In brief, these objectives are (1) to minimize or neutralize the effects of any future flooding by complying with Federal, State and local requirements regarding areas subject to flooding (this includes a commitment by the locality to adopt flood plain ordinances), (2) correct or compensate for physical damage to both private and public property, and to (3) generally upgrade the area with regard to essential neighborhood services, private property rehabilitation, traffic control, parking, utilities, open spaces, recreation, shopping, etc.
Although item (3) above may be in addition to the direct needs of the community to recover from the storm damage, these additional activities are viewed as necessary due to the vehicle by which assistance is given the community, i.e., urban renewal. These items are necessary to protect the Federal investment in the area provided under items (1) and (2) and are consistent with urban renewal practices allowed under Title I of the Housing Act of 1949.
3. Summary of Environmental impact and adverse environmental effects:
In summary there are no major items of an adverse nature that would preclude the approval of the plan as represented in the Draft EIS. None of the responding agencies listed below in paragraph 5, indicated or recommended disapproval due to adverse environmental factors that would be brought about by project activity. We also conclude that no combination of minor adverse consequences would preclude the project. Balanced against the negative aspects of the project is a number of positive aspects that will be realized by the project activity.
Some of the minor negative environmental effects are:
a. Minor irrevocable commitment of natural resources
b. Slight air and water pollution caused by project construction and demolition.
c. Some loss to the tax base due to public acquisition of private property.
d. Inconvenience to project residents during relocation activities.
e. Damage of loss to rehabilitation property during subsequent flooding due to location within the 100 year flood plain.
4. Alternatives Considered:
a. No public action
b. More flood control
c. Radical clearance and demolition in the flood plain area
